diagnosis: Acute appendicitis
procedure: Laparoscopic appendectomy
treatment_notes: He reached the casualty ward at about 11 pm with severe pain low on the right side of his belly and repeated vomiting. A scan showed an inflamed appendix and he was operated on that same night. He stayed three nights in a single private room (around 6,500 a day) and went home on the fourth day. His wife rang the insurer's helpline at 9 the next morning to let them know.
rationale: A genuine emergency admission needs no pre-authorization (7.1) and the insurer was told within 24 hours (7.2). Appendicitis is not a specified condition, cover is over four years old, and the room rate is under the daily cap.

diagnosis: Cloudy lens in the right eye (cataract)
procedure: Phacoemulsification with standard foldable lens, right eye
treatment_notes: Her vision in the right eye had been getting steadily blurrier over about two years. The operation was done under eye drops at a hospital on the insurer's cashless list, and she walked out the same afternoon. The insurer had approved the surgery in writing a week before.
rationale: Cataract is on the 24-month specified-condition list, and 24 months from 2024-10-20 ends on 2026-10-20. Surgery on 2026-10-12 falls 8 days short, so the claim is not payable.

diagnosis: Recurring severe headaches (migraine)
procedure: Video-call consultation with a neurologist and e-prescription
treatment_notes: Ananya lives far from the nearest neurologist, so she had a 20-minute video call with a registered specialist who is based in another city. The doctor went through her symptoms on screen and sent a digital prescription for tablets, which she bought at a chemist. There was no in-person visit at any point.
rationale: The outpatient benefit pays a registered doctor's consultation fee against a prescription, but the policy never says whether a remote consultation counts. This is a planted gap, so a human reviewer should decide.

diagnosis: Dengue fever with falling platelet count
procedure: IV fluids and daily platelet monitoring
treatment_notes: After five days of high fever he became very weak and his blood count dropped, so the doctor admitted him for drips and monitoring. He stayed four nights in a private room billed at 6,500 a day and did not need intensive care. The hospital got cashless approval from the insurer the same morning and he was discharged fully recovered. The bill splits into room rent 26,000, doctor visits and nursing 18,000, and tests and medicines 34,000.
rationale: Admission on 2026-09-12 is day 33 of cover, past the 30-day initial wait. The room costs more than the Plan A cap of 5,000 a day, so room rent is paid at 20,000 and doctor and nursing charges at about 77% (13,846), plus tests and medicines in full, giving 67,846 payable.

diagnosis: Deep scald burns to left forearm and hand (hot oil)
procedure: Skin graft and scar-release plastic surgery
treatment_notes: About four months ago a pan of hot oil spilled over her left arm in the kitchen and caused deep burns. They healed with tight scars that stopped her from straightening her fingers fully. A plastic surgeon grafted skin and loosened the scar tissue, and she stayed two nights. The insurer had approved the admission beforehand.
rationale: Plastic surgery is normally excluded by 10.2, but 10.2.1(b) carves out burn treatment including reconstructive surgery after burns. The surgery is repair of burn damage, not a cosmetic enhancement, so the exception applies.

diagnosis: Typhoid fever
procedure: Injectable antibiotics and IV fluids
treatment_notes: He had five days of fever and stomach upset, and a blood test confirmed typhoid. He was admitted for three nights for antibiotic injections and discharged much better. This was his first policy with the insurer and he had bought it less than a month earlier.
rationale: The admission began on day 27 of cover, inside the 30-day initial waiting period for illness. It was not an accident, so the accident exemption in 8.2 does not help.

diagnosis: Pneumonia
procedure: Antibiotic drips and oxygen support
treatment_notes: After a week of cough and breathlessness his family doctor advised admission, and he went to a hospital five minutes from home. He stayed five nights in an ordinary private room at 4,500 a day. That hospital is not on the cashless list, although a listed hospital exists about 12 km away. The family paid the bill and is claiming it back, having phoned the insurer beforehand and got a go-ahead.
rationale: The illness is covered and all waits are long served, but he is over 60 (20% co-pay) and treated at a non-network hospital (10% co-pay). The two add up to 30% under 11.8, so 70% of 1,65,000 (115,500) is payable; no emergency waiver applies because a capable network hospital was nearby.

diagnosis: Fainting spells, cause under investigation
procedure: Overnight tests: brain scan, heart tracing, blood work
treatment_notes: She had two fainting episodes within a week, so her doctor had her admitted for a full round of tests. She was kept in the ward for about 30 hours for scans, heart monitoring and blood tests. Everything came back normal, no medicine or procedure was given, and she was sent home to follow up at the clinic.
rationale: The stay passed 24 hours but was purely for investigation with no active treatment, so it is not Hospitalization under 1.5.3. 10.11 excludes diagnostic-only admissions, and its exception needs treatment to follow in the same admission, which did not happen.

diagnosis: Right inguinal hernia
procedure: Laparoscopic hernia mesh repair
treatment_notes: He had a bulge in his right groin for about six years and wrote it down when he bought the policy. It became painful, and the surgeon fixed it with a keyhole operation. He went home the same evening after roughly nine hours. He has been continuously insured for a little over two years.
rationale: Hernia is on the 24-month list and that wait is met at just under 28 months, but it was declared as pre-existing. 8.5 makes the longer 36-month wait in 9.1 apply instead, and that runs until 2027-06-15.

diagnosis: Broken left thigh bone (femur) in a road accident
procedure: Surgical fixation with a metal rod
treatment_notes: A car hit his scooter on the way to work and an ambulance (2,400) took him straight to the nearest hospital, where X-rays showed a broken thigh bone. He was operated on the next morning and stayed six nights. His policy had been running for only nine days. His brother informed the insurer that same evening.
rationale: Day 9 of cover is inside the 30-day initial wait, but 8.2 exempts treatment that results directly from an accident. It was an emergency, so no pre-authorization was needed (7.1), and the ambulance charge is under its limit.

diagnosis: Long-standing lower back pain
procedure: Six weekly acupuncture sessions given by a doctor
treatment_notes: For months of back pain she went to the pain-management department of a large city hospital, where a physician offered a course of needle (acupuncture) sessions. The physician is fully registered with the state medical council and holds an extra certificate in acupuncture. She attended six weekly sessions, got a receipt for each, and the doctor wrote a letter recommending the course. No medicines or scans were prescribed.
rationale: The practitioner is a registered doctor and the amount fits within the remaining Plan A outpatient limit (5,000 less 1,200 already used), so those points are settled. But clause 5.1 pays consultation fees, tests and medicines and never says whether repeated procedure-type therapy such as acupuncture counts, and AYUSH (1.13) is defined only for in-patient care. This is a planted gap that a human reviewer should decide.

diagnosis: Spreading skin infection of the right lower leg (cellulitis)
procedure: Antibiotic drips
treatment_notes: His leg was red, hot and swollen, and at a morning clinic visit the doctor recommended drips, so he was admitted at 4 pm. His fever settled quickly and he went home at noon the next day, about 20 hours later, on tablets. This was a planned admission, not an ambulance or casualty arrival.
rationale: A stay of about 20 hours is under the 24-hour minimum for Hospitalization (1.5.1). IV antibiotics for cellulitis is not a short-stay procedure of the kind that 1.5.2 exempts, so the claim is not payable.

diagnosis: Cataract in the left eye
procedure: Cataract surgery with a premium multifocal lens
treatment_notes: His left eye had gone cloudy, and he chose a premium lens so he could manage without reading glasses. The operation was done under eye drops and he left the same day. The bill lumps together the surgeon, theatre, lens and follow-up checks within the month. The same hospital charges about 38,000 for this surgery with a standard lens.
rationale: Cover is over three years old, so the 24-month cataract wait is long met. The per-eye cap on Plan B is 30,000 and only a standard lens is payable, so approve up to 30,000 and the premium-lens excess falls on the insured.

diagnosis: Pregnancy growing in the fallopian tube that has burst (ruptured ectopic)
procedure: Emergency keyhole surgery to remove the affected tube
treatment_notes: At around seven weeks pregnant she collapsed with sharp lower belly pain and dizziness and was rushed to hospital. A scan showed the pregnancy had grown in the tube and ruptured, so she was operated on at once and stayed three nights. Her husband told the insurer the next morning.
rationale: Delivery-type maternity cover needs 24 months (8.4), but 6.4 says 'notwithstanding 8.4' that complications arising before labour, including ectopic pregnancy, are paid as an ordinary illness. Only the 30-day initial wait applies, which was met at about eight months, and the maternity caps do not apply.

diagnosis: Infected non-healing foot sore due to diabetes
procedure: Surgical wound cleaning and removal of one toe
treatment_notes: His long-standing sugar problem led to a sore on his right foot that would not heal and became infected. Surgeons cleaned out the wound and had to remove one toe, and he stayed nine nights. He had written down his diabetes on the form when he bought the policy two years ago, and the admission was approved in advance.
rationale: A diabetic foot infection is a direct complication of declared diabetes, which 9.3 treats as part of that pre-existing condition. The 36-month wait (to 2027-08-12) has not run, as cover is only about 26 months old.

diagnosis: Two chipped upper front teeth after a cycling fall
procedure: Tooth-coloured filling material built up on the two chipped teeth
treatment_notes: Aarav fell off his bike on a rough road and chipped two of his own front teeth, with a small cut on the lip. A dentist at the dental department of a nearby listed hospital saw him within hours that same evening and rebuilt both teeth in one sitting. He had never had any dental work on those teeth before.
rationale: Dental treatment is excluded by 10.3, but 10.3.1 restores cover for repair of natural teeth damaged in an accident when treatment starts within 90 days. Here it started the same day, and the amount is under the 10,000 per-accident outpatient limit.

diagnosis: Prostate cancer confined to the gland
procedure: Robot-assisted removal of the prostate
treatment_notes: After his biopsy the surgeon removed the prostate using a robotic system, which means smaller cuts and usually a quicker recovery. He stayed three nights in a private room. The bill shows a separate line of about 1,10,000 for 'robotic system use and instruments' on top of the usual surgeon and theatre charges.
rationale: Cancer surgery is clearly covered and waits are served, but the policy never mentions robotic assistance. Whether the robotic-use surcharge is a reasonable and customary charge or an excluded non-medical or consumable item is undefined; a 20% age co-pay also applies at age 61.

diagnosis: Severe stomach infection with dehydration
procedure: IV fluids and injectable medicines
treatment_notes: She was admitted on 7 May 2026 with vomiting and loose motions and was discharged on 10 May after three nights on drips. She paid the hospital herself and posted the original bills and discharge papers to the insurer only on 2 September 2026. She says she was busy with work and kept putting it off; there was no illness or other obstacle.
rationale: Documents were due within 30 days of discharge (by 2026-06-09), and even with condonation the outer limit is 90 days (2026-08-08). They arrived on day 115 with no genuine documented reason, so the claim is time-barred.

diagnosis: 8 mm kidney stone stuck in the left ureter
procedure: Laser stone breaking through a telescope with a temporary stent
treatment_notes: He had repeated attacks of severe flank pain and the stone would not pass on its own. The surgery was booked with the hospital a week ahead, but the family only told the insurer on the morning of the operation. He was home by evening, about eight hours after arriving.
rationale: Stone treatment is a specified condition, but cover is over three years old so the 24-month wait is met. It was planned, so approval was needed 72 hours ahead (13.2); with none obtained and no impracticality shown, cashless is unavailable and the payable amount is reduced by 10% (13.4.1) to 79,200, not rejected.

diagnosis: Heart attack
procedure: Emergency angioplasty with one stent, plus ambulance transfer
treatment_notes: Mr Rao had crushing chest pain on a family trip to a hill town and was taken by ambulance to the only hospital nearby, which is not on the insurer's cashless list. The nearest listed hospital was about 85 km away by road. He had an urgent stent the same night and stayed four nights. The ambulance charged 3,000 and the family told the insurer the next morning.
rationale: In an emergency where the nearest network hospital is over 20 km away, the 10% non-network co-pay is waived (7.5). Ambulance is paid up to 3,000 under 7.3, which prevails over the general 2,000 cap in 11.4 as 11.9 directs.

diagnosis: Wear-and-tear arthritis in both knees
procedure: Injection of her own bone-marrow stem cells into both knee joints
treatment_notes: She wanted to avoid knee replacement, so a clinic drew bone marrow from her hip and injected the concentrated cells into both knees. She stayed two nights for the procedure and rest. The clinic itself calls it a regenerative treatment that is still being studied, and the bill is a single package fee. The admission form was cleared by the insurer's helpdesk, which noted that treatment suitability had not been assessed.
rationale: The policy has no clause on stem-cell or other regenerative therapy and no explicit experimental-treatment exclusion. Only the Medical Necessity test (generally accepted practice) in 1.7 bears on it, and the pre-authorization is not a final admission of liability (12.4), so a clinician must judge it.

diagnosis: Unhappy with nose shape; no breathing problem
procedure: Nose reshaping with a chin implant
treatment_notes: Tanvi had no injury and no breathing trouble but wanted a more refined nose and a stronger chin line. The surgery was done under general anaesthesia and she stayed one night. Her surgeon's letter confirms it was done only to change her appearance.
rationale: Surgery done for appearance is excluded by 10.2. None of the exceptions in 10.2.1 (accident reconstruction, burns, post-cancer reconstruction) fits.

diagnosis: Full-term pregnancy, normal vaginal birth
procedure: Normal delivery with a two-night stay
treatment_notes: She went into labour at 39 weeks and had an uncomplicated vaginal birth of a healthy baby girl. Mother and baby stayed two nights in a private room. The hospital package covers delivery, doctor and nursing fees, and she is also claiming scans and check-ups from the pregnancy. She had told the insurer about the hospital and due date six weeks earlier.
rationale: The 24-month maternity wait is met (about 27 months) and this is her first claimed delivery. The Plan B normal-delivery limit of 60,000 covers everything including room and pre/post-natal costs, so approve up to 60,000 and the 11,000 excess falls on the insured.

diagnosis: Blocked heart arteries in all three main vessels
procedure: Open-heart bypass surgery
treatment_notes: He came in with chest pain on walking and had bypass surgery, staying eight nights. The hospital's old records show a stent was placed for blocked arteries in 2023 and that he has been on heart medicines since. The form he filled in for this policy had 'no' ticked against heart disease.
rationale: Heart disease treated in 2023 falls within the 48 months before inception, so it is pre-existing (1.9), and the 36-month wait is only about 19 months along (9.1). Failing to disclose it also lets the insurer refuse the claim (15.1), and the 60-month moratorium has not been reached.

diagnosis: Hip fracture after a fall at home, in recovery
procedure: Daily nurse visits at home for three weeks after discharge
treatment_notes: She slipped in her bathroom, broke her hip and was operated on, then discharged after six days; the insurer has already paid that hospital bill. Her surgeon prescribed a nurse to visit daily for three weeks for injections, dressings and first exercises at home. This claim is only for the nursing agency's charges.
rationale: After-discharge cover lists consultations, medicines and tests but never names home nursing, and the domiciliary benefit covers treatment at home instead of a hospital stay, not post-discharge care. The policy is silent, so it needs review (a 20% age co-pay would also apply if allowed).

diagnosis: Perforated stomach ulcer with infection of the belly lining
procedure: Emergency open surgery to close the perforation
treatment_notes: She came to casualty late at night with sudden severe belly pain and a rigid abdomen and was taken straight to theatre. She stayed four nights. Single rooms at the standard rate were free, but the family chose a deluxe room at 12,500 a day. The bill: room rent 50,000, surgeon and anaesthetist fees 80,000, operation theatre 25,000, medicines 40,000 and tests 15,000. Her son informed the insurer the next morning. Her policy carries the 25,000 voluntary deductible and nothing has been claimed this year.
rationale: Room rent is capped at 10,000 a day on Plan B, so the room is paid at 40,000 and the room-linked charges (surgeon and anaesthetist 80,000, theatre 25,000) are scaled by 10,000/12,500 = 0.8 to 64,000 and 20,000; medicines and tests are not room-linked and stay whole. Step 2 total is 179,000. Step 3 takes off the 25,000 deductible leaving 154,000, and only then Step 4 applies the 20% age co-pay (she is over 60), giving 123,200. Applying the co-pay before the deductible would wrongly give 118,200. The proportionate deduction exception for unavailable rooms does not apply because cheaper rooms were free.

diagnosis: Severe kidney infection that spread to the blood with a dangerous drop in blood pressure
procedure: Intensive care with IV antibiotics and blood pressure support
treatment_notes: He was brought in by his wife with high fever, shaking and fainting, and was moved straight to the intensive care unit, where he stayed four days at 14,000 a day. He then spent two days in an ordinary private room at 4,500 a day. Doctors' fees came to 60,000 and medicines and tests to 70,000. The family called the insurer from the hospital the same afternoon.
rationale: Intensive care is paid up to its own daily limit (2% of the Sum Insured, 10,000 a day on Plan A), not the room rent limit, so 4 x 14,000 = 56,000 is paid at 40,000. The ward room at 4,500 is under the 5,000 room cap, so no proportionate deduction applies to the doctors' fees, and intensive care is exempt from it in any case. Payable is 40,000 + 9,000 + 60,000 + 70,000 = 179,000.

diagnosis: Broken ankle after a slip on a hiking trail
procedure: Surgery to fix the ankle bones with a metal plate and screws
treatment_notes: On a weekend group trek in the Western Ghats he slipped on wet rock at about 2,600 metres and badly broke his ankle. Friends carried him down and took him to a hospital on the insurer's cashless list, where he was operated on that night and stayed three nights in a room at 6,000 a day. The trek's highest point, according to the organiser's GPS log, was 2,900 metres. A friend phoned the insurer the next morning.
rationale: The hazardous-activities exclusion covers mountaineering above 3,000 metres and expressly leaves ordinary trekking below that height outside the exclusion. This trek peaked at 2,900 metres, so 10.8 does not apply. The fracture surgery is a covered Accident claim, the plate and screws are covered implants, the room is within the cap, and an emergency admission needs no pre-authorization.

diagnosis: Full-term pregnancy, baby in breech position, planned caesarean
procedure: Planned caesarean delivery with a four-night stay
treatment_notes: This is her third baby. Her first was born in February 2020, about eight months after she bought the policy, and that bill was turned down as too early so the family paid it themselves. The insurer did pay the maternity claim for her second baby in September 2022. This time the baby is lying feet-first, so the surgeon booked a caesarean, and she gave the insurer the hospital name and date nine weeks ahead. The bill of 104,000 covers the surgery and stay, plus scans and check-ups during pregnancy.
rationale: A delivery counts toward the two-delivery lifetime limit only once a maternity benefit has actually been paid for it. Only one benefit (2022) has been paid, since the first delivery was refused during the waiting period, so this is effectively the second counted delivery and is still payable. The 24-month maternity wait is long met, so the caesarean is paid up to the Plan B limit of 90,000 inclusive of everything in 6.1, and the 14,000 above it falls on the insured.

diagnosis: Cracked upper front tooth after a fall on the stairs
procedure: Root canal and a cap on the cracked tooth
treatment_notes: He tripped on the stairs at home on 4 August and cracked a healthy front tooth, with no other injury. He was travelling for work, so he only saw a dentist in the dental department of a large hospital on 3 September, where the tooth was saved with a root canal and a cap. He had never had work on that tooth before. The bill is 9,500.
rationale: Dental treatment is excluded by 10.3, and 10.3.1 restores cover for accident-damaged natural teeth if treatment starts within 90 days; this began on day 30. But 10.3.1 says the outpatient payment is 'within the limit in clause 7.6', and 7.6 itself covers emergency-department treatment only within 24 hours of the Accident. The policy does not say whether 7.6's 24-hour condition travels with its amount, so a reviewer must decide.
